Saquon Barkley Says the NFL Forced Him to Divest His Polymarket Stake

Published November 2, 2026 · 4 min read · By the OddsLighthouse Editorial Team

Philadelphia Eagles running back Saquon Barkley says the NFL required him to give up an equity stake he held in Polymarket, the prediction-market platform, because the league treats investment in prediction markets the same way it treats investment in sportsbooks. "I am not in that right now," Barkley told Front Office Sports. "I am not allowed to be in that."

What Barkley said

Barkley said the league informs players each year, before the season starts, about what they can and cannot do with respect to endorsements, investments, and outside business activities, and that prediction-market companies now fall under the same restrictions as sportsbooks. "So I kinda had to get out of that," he said, adding: "I was in it before, but no bueno." Barkley's stake in Polymarket had previously surfaced publicly as part of a broader profile of his outside investments. Front Office Sports did not report a dollar figure for the stake or the date he divested it.

The NFL's position

The NFL confirmed to Front Office Sports that it prohibits players from investing in or promoting sportsbooks and prediction markets, but it declined to comment specifically on Barkley's situation. An NFLPA spokesperson has separately said the league views prediction-market companies as gambling entities under its existing gambling policy, meaning a player can't serve as an endorser or brand ambassador for a company like Kalshi or Polymarket any more than for a licensed sportsbook. The NFL has also opposed prediction-market advertising during its broadcasts, barring prediction-market Super Bowl ads last season, and has urged the Supreme Court to let sports event contracts be regulated at the state level rather than federally.

Why it matters

The NFL's stance is notably stricter than at least one other major league's: the NBA this week named Kalshi and Polymarket as preferred prediction-market partners, and NBA players are not barred from investing in or endorsing prediction-market platforms, only from promoting NBA-specific event contracts. That split underscores how unevenly US sports leagues are treating prediction markets even as the platforms keep signing athletes and league-level deals — Kalshi has reported deals with other prominent athletes, and MLB struck its own exclusive prediction-market agreement with Polymarket earlier this year. For bettors and fans, the episode is a reminder that prediction markets occupy a genuinely unsettled space: leagues, state regulators, and the platforms themselves still don't agree on whether they should be treated as gambling, and that disagreement is now shaping what even the athletes on the field are allowed to own.
